title: Somadatta's End (Day 14)
body:
Somadatta's End (Day 14)

मया हतम्पूर्वमेव निमित्तमात्रं भव सव्यसाचिन् ॥

Translation: They have already been slain by Me; be you merely an instrument, O Savyasachin (ambidextrous bowman). (Bhagavad Gita 11.33)

The fourteenth day of the Kurukshetra War witnessed unprecedented violence and desperate tactics. Recognising that Arjuna's failure to slay Jayadratha would result in his self-immolation—thereby securing an absolute, effortless victory for the Kauravas—Dronacharya arranged his forces in a triple-layered formation (a circular array backed by a lotus array, which was further supported by a spike-headed force), keeping Jayadratha hidden twelve miles in the rear under the heavy guard of Ashwatthama, Kripa, and Karna.
Arjuna advanced like the Destroyer incarnate, his ambidextrous hands discharging a continuous, dark cloud of arrows from the Gandiva, annihilating an entire Akshauhini of Kuru forces in his path. As the afternoon progressed and the horses grew weary, Sree Krishna paused to unyoke and refresh them, while Arjuna erected a protective fortress of arrows around them. In another part of the field, a deadly ancestral feud flared up between Satyaki and Bhurisravas, the son of Somadatta, whose families had been bound in hostility since Somadatta's duel with Sini over the hand of Devaki. Bhurisravas, an unrivalled swordsman, overpowered the exhausted Satyaki, dragging him across the ground and raising his sword to deliver the final strike.
Sree Krishna, watching the crisis, urged Arjuna to intervene. Though Arjuna felt a deep ethical conflict in striking a warrior who was not actively engaged with him, he steeled his heart to protect his devoted disciple and discharged a lightning-swift shaft that severed Bhurisravas's uplifted right arm. The old warrior, bitterly denouncing Arjuna for committing the cowardly act of striking from behind, spread his arrows on the ground and sat in a silent Yoga posture to release his soul. As the assembly looked on in awe, the impetuous Satyaki, driven by unchecked wrath, rushed forward and struck off the meditating preceptor's head—an act of raw, unbridled passion that drew universal condemnation from the field, proving that once the banks of Dharma are breached, the flood of adharma spares no one.
As the sun sloped rapidly toward the western horizon, Jayadratha remained safely out of Arjuna's reach, and the Kauravas began to exult in anticipation of Arjuna's defeat. It was then that Sree Krishna, the supreme master of material energy (Prakriti), utilized His divine power to obscure the sun, simulating a premature sunset. Believing the day was done and they were victorious, the Kuru warriors dropped their guard, and Jayadratha stepped forward, laughing in derision to watch Arjuna enter the flames.
Sree Krishna instantly withdrew the shadow and commanded Arjuna to strike. Sree Krishna warned him that Jayadratha's father, Vriddhakshatra, had pronounced a curse that whoever caused his son's head to fall to the earth would have his own head burst into a hundred fragments. With supreme precision, Arjuna discharged a crescent-headed shaft that severed Jayadratha's head and kept it suspended in the air with a succession of swift arrows, carrying it twelve miles away to drop directly into the lap of Vriddhakshatra, who was engaged in evening prayers in his forest hermitage. As the startled father rose, the head fell to the ground, and Vriddhakshatra's own head instantly burst into fragments, fulfilling the cosmic circle of karma.
